paper.authors_full: Ziyang Huang, Jiajia Zhao, Xuan Fu
paper.title: Generative AI as an External Cognitive Tool for Developing Creative Intelligence in Visual Design: A Mixed-Methods Randomized Study Using Cognitive Load Indicators and Motivational Modeling
paper.pdf_filename: Huang Zhao Fu (2026) - Generative AI as an External Cognitive Tool for Developing Creative Intelligence.pdf
paper.version_read: Journal version of record, J. Intell. 2026, 14, 65; published 14 April 2026; DOI 10.3390/jintelligence14040065 (PDF p. 1).
paper.one_line_finding: Across 24 group projects, instruction integrating GenAI throughout design thinking had higher overall expert scores than traditional instruction with sporadic GenAI (86.58 [SD 1.84] vs 79.94 [SD 2.98]; t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001, d = 2.68; p. 20, Section 4.6).

studies.label: Six-week illustration course experiment (GenAI-integrated vs traditional instruction)
studies.cluster_se_treatment: The reported independent-sample t-test treats projects as observations; no adjustment for instructional classes/sessions or student dependence is reported (PDF p. 20, Section 4.6). Separate classes delivered the two arms (PDF p. 9, Section 3.4.1); the number of independent instructional clusters per arm is not printed.

arms.name: Experimental (Integrated Teaching Model)
arms.description: GenAI embedded throughout the design-thinking stages with explicit tool-intervention points, workshops, group collaboration, iterative production, and process feedback (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 3.4.3 and Table 2). Analyzed people count is for questionnaires, not a confirmed count of contributors to the rated projects.

arms.name: Control (Traditional Teaching Model)
arms.description: Traditional lecturer-led instruction and case analysis, primarily independent assignments and final-outcome evaluation; GenAI used sporadically for sketch generation, style reference, or material preparation, with manual drawing and conventional digital software dominant (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 3.4.3 and Table 2). Analyzed people count is for questionnaires, not a confirmed count of contributors to the rated projects.

studies.task: Complete final group illustration-design projects during a six-week Illustration Design course, submitting final images, design statements, and process summaries for expert evaluation.

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Runway, and unspecified AIGC/emotion-analysis tools
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 7, Figure 2, GenAI Application boxes (visually checked in memory after page-text extraction). ChatGPT, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, and Runway are named; AIGC and AI for emotion analysis are not further specified. Intervention model versions and release years are not printed. PDF p. 9, Section 3.4.2 names DALL·E and ChatGPT-4 as prior-use survey examples only.

preregistration.where: No preregistration is identified in the complete article.

estimates.outcome: Overall expert evaluation score of final project (mean of five dimensions)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Six experts with teaching and industry experience in illustration and visual communication rated anonymized final group projects, presented in randomized order, on a 100-point scale (PDF pp. 11-12, Section 3.5.1; PDF p. 20, Section 4.6). The overall project score is the mean across Creativity, Applicability, Technicality, Expressiveness, and Completeness. This composite assesses the quality of final design outcomes (PDF p. 20, Section 4.6), so it is coded usefulness under codebook Section 6.

estimates.notes: The people contributing to the rated projects are not enumerated, and project membership, team sizes, and team formation are not reported; participant counts for this analysis are therefore null. The student-level questionnaire/SEM counts cannot be substituted for project contributors. The article reports individual student allocation followed by instruction in separate classes by arm. The study assignment unit is session under extraction rule 9, despite the individual-allocation wording. The number of independent instructional clusters is unreported; the rated projects must not be used as cluster counts. Cluster replication required for core eligibility remains unconfirmed. The article does not establish whether the tabulated means use initial independent ratings or scores after discussion to consensus (PDF pp. 12, 20-21). Higher values mean better quality of the final design output, so higher_is is more_creative under the usefulness construct. Means, SDs, the t-test, and Cohen’s d are transcribed exactly as printed. The paper does not specify the standardizer for d. The independent-sample test treats projects as observations and reports no participant- or class-adjusted uncertainty, so se_basis is output. No mean difference, SE, or interval has been calculated. The composite is coded usefulness because it measures the quality of a creative design output (PDF p. 20, Section 4.6; codebook Section 6). Its output-level uncertainty and unresolved instructional-cluster replication remain limitations.

not_extracted.what: PLS-SEM direct paths, moderation, and multi-group path comparisons
not_extracted.reason: Associations among post-treatment questionnaire constructs and moderation analyses, not full-sample treatment contrasts on output-scored creativity; measurement-model diagnostics likewise are not output outcomes (PDF pp. 17-19, Sections 4.3-4.5.1 and Table 11).

not_extracted.what: Supplementary indirect paths and between-group indirect-effect comparisons
not_extracted.reason: Mediation/indirect-effect analyses of questionnaire constructs are excluded (PDF p. 20, Section 4.5.2 and Table 12).

not_extracted.what: Lecturer, learner, and expert qualitative interview findings
not_extracted.reason: Qualitative experiences, perceptions, and explanatory observations; no independently scored quantitative creative-output contrast (PDF p. 13, Section 3.5.3; PDF p. 21, Section 4.6; PDF p. 23, Section 4.7).

not_extracted.what: Questionnaire psychometrics, measurement invariance, and expert inter-rater reliability
not_extracted.reason: Reliability, validity, and measurement-invariance statistics are measurement diagnostics, not differences between randomized arms on creative output. Expert ICC confidence intervals must not be entered as outcome-effect intervals (PDF pp. 16-18, Tables 8-10; PDF p. 22, Table 14).

open_items: Instructional-cluster replication is not established. The paper reports individual allocation but separate classes for the arms (PDF p. 9, Section 3.4.1). Applying extraction rule 9 gives assignment_unit=session. The number of independent classes/sessions per arm is not printed, so clusters_per_arm is null for each arm; do not infer one class per arm or count repeated teaching weeks as independent randomized clusters. The codebook requirement for replicated clusters must be resolved before treating this study as core-eligible. field_rct describes the reported randomized coursework experiment; it does not certify that the cluster-replication criterion is met.

The number of distinct students represented by the rated projects, project-to-student membership, team sizes, team formation, and possible dependence among projects are not reported. Study and arm analyzed counts refer to the questionnaire/SEM samples; all creative-output contrast people counts remain null (PDF pp. 12, 15, 20-21).

No participant-level outcome SD or participant-adjusted uncertainty is printed. The only numerical creative-output contrast uses an independent-sample project-level t-test; this output-level uncertainty does not establish participant-level precision (PDF p. 20, Section 4.6).

The Creativity, Applicability, Technicality, Expressiveness, and Completeness dimensions have project-specific means but no printed arm summaries or numerical contrast statistics. Such summaries would require separate computation from the printed project data, which is outside transcription (PDF p. 21, Table 13; PDF p. 22, Figure 6).
The standardizing denominator for the reported Cohen’s d is not specified (PDF p. 20, Section 4.6).

The paper describes independent expert ratings followed by discussion to consensus, but does not specify whether the project means, outcome test, or ICCs use initial or consensus ratings (PDF pp. 20-22, Section 4.6 and Tables 13-14).

The prose calls Figure 6 scatter points individual expert ratings, but the plotted values appear compatible with project means; the point unit is unresolved. No figure-derived numerical statistic is recorded (PDF pp. 21-22).
The intervention model versions and release years are not stated. Tool names come from Figure 2; baseline-survey examples do not establish intervention model versions (PDF pp. 7, 9).
The study location is anonymized as College X; participant country is not stated. The author affiliation and ethics institution do not establish the recruitment location (PDF pp. 1, 9, 28).
